2027-05-21.title: First Friday of the Apostles · The Friday of Gold
2027-05-21.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: A lame man is healed by the apostles
The blind see and the lame walk
2027-05-21.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe). Pentecost opened the seven weeks of this season, which recalls the birth of the Church and the mission of the apostles. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angelus (“The Angel of the Lord”) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The Friday of Gold, the first Friday after Pentecost, an ordinary feast of the Oriental tradition, recalls the healing of the man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple (Acts 3), the first miracle worked by the apostles after the coming of the Spirit. The calendar notes that if only two readings are chosen, it is proper to read from the Acts of the Apostles. Longer forms in the calendar: 1 Corinthians 12:28–13:13; Luke 7:1–23.
2027-05-21.verse: But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.”
theo: On the first Friday after Pentecost the Churches of the Syriac tradition keep a feast with a shining name: the Friday of Gold. It looks back to the first sign worked by the apostles after the Holy Spirit came upon them. Peter and John go up to the Temple “at the hour of prayer, at three o’clock in the afternoon”, the hour at which, only weeks before, Jesus had died on the Cross. At the gate called Beautiful lies a man “lame from birth”, carried there daily to beg. He asks for alms. “Peter looked intently at him, as did John, and said, ‘Look at us.’” Then comes the sentence that gives the day its name, as it is commonly explained: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.” The Church of the apostles is poor in gold and rich in the Name. Peter takes the man by the right hand, raises him, and “immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.” The man enters the Temple “walking and leaping and praising God.” The man lame from birth, more than forty years old (Acts 4:22), who had lain outside the gate, now goes in. Pentecost is not only a wind and tongues of fire; it is a hand stretched out to a beggar at the door.

Isaiah had seen this day from afar. To exiles worn out by grief he cried: “Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who are of a fearful heart, ‘Be strong, do not fear! Here is your God.’” And then: “the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless sing for joy.” The prophet sees a desert blooming, waters breaking out in the wilderness, and a road through it called “the Holy Way”, on which “the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with singing.” In Acts 3 that prophecy walks into the Temple on healed feet. The lame man leaping at the Beautiful Gate is a living sign that the age of the Messiah has begun, and that the Holy Way now runs through the Church of the apostles. Every parish that welcomes the weak, the disabled, the forgotten, and helps them go in to the house of God is walking that road.

Peter then speaks to the crowd in Solomon’s Portico. He refuses all credit: “why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?” The healing is the work of “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our ancestors”, who “has glorified his servant Jesus.” Peter speaks as a son of Israel to his own people, and his words about the Passion are hard. But notice how he continues: “And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” He does not condemn; he calls to repentance and blessing: “Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out, so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord.” And he ends with the promise to Abraham: “in your descendants all the families of the earth shall be blessed”, adding that God sent his servant “first to you, to bless you.” The Church has always read these words without blaming the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Christ (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). It is our sins, the sins of all, that brought the Lord to the Cross, and it is to all of us that the times of refreshing are offered.

Why does the calendar join to this feast Paul's hymn to love? Because the healing at the gate was an act of love before it was an act of power. Paul has just listed the gifts of the Spirit, and now he says, “strive for the greater gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.” Without love, tongues are “a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal”; prophecy, knowledge and faith that moves mountains are nothing; even giving away all possessions gains nothing. “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude… It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never ends.” Peter had no gold, but he had this. He looked at the beggar, which the passers-by never did; he said, “Look at us”; he took him by the hand. The gold of this Friday is not the gold Peter lacked. It is love, which outlasts prophecies and tongues and knowledge: “And now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; and the greatest of these is love.”

The Gospel shows us where the apostles learned this. At the gate of the town of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral: “He was his mother’s only son, and she was a widow.” Before any request is made, “When the Lord saw her, he had compassion for her and said to her, ‘Do not weep.’” He touches the bier, the bearers stand still, and he says, “Young man, I say to you, rise!” and “Jesus gave him to his mother.” When John the Baptist's disciples come to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another?”, Jesus answers with Isaiah's own words: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them.” The gate of Nain and the Beautiful Gate belong together: what Jesus did at one gate, his apostles do at the other in his Name. In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns that she has no treasure of her own to give the world, only Christ, and that he is enough. The gold of our Church is not in her buildings or her accounts, but in the Name of Jesus spoken with love to someone lying at the door.
conn: The lame shall leap like a deer.
Isaiah 35:6 is fulfilled at the Beautiful Gate: the man enters “walking and leaping and praising God” (Acts 3:8).
Hebrews takes up Isaiah 35:3: “Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees” (Hebrews 12:12).
Before the council Peter explains the healing: “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).
Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15: “The Lord your God will raise up for you from your own people a prophet like me” (Acts 3:22).
“In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), recalled by Peter in Acts 3:25.
At Zarephath Elijah raised a widow's son and “gave him to his mother” (1 Kings 17:23); Luke uses the same words at Nain (Luke 7:15).
Jesus' answer to John repeats Isaiah 35:5–6 and Isaiah 61:1: good news to the poor.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the Church, poor in silver and gold, gives what she has: the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, in whose Name the weak are made strong.
Peter and John went up to the Temple at the hour of prayer: the apostles' first sign came from the rhythm of prayer. From our Qurbana and our hours of prayer the strength comes to raise others up.
outline: A beggar at a beautiful gate, and two apostles with empty pockets.
Isaiah's Holy Way and the lame who leap like a deer.
Point 2 · What I have I give you

live: Look at the one at the gate (Acts 3:4)
Today, look into the eyes of one person you usually pass by, and speak to them.
You may have no money to give; give time, a visit, a phone call, a prayer said with someone.
Ask how your parish can help the disabled and elderly to come in: a ramp, a seat, someone to accompany them.
Put your own name in place of ‘love’ and see where you fall short; ask the Spirit for that gift.
fathers: See the poverty of Peter and his wealth: he had no money, yet he gave what money cannot buy. Had he given silver, the man would soon have spent it and remained lame; he gave him his feet, and with his feet the praise of God.

Love, and do what you will: if you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing but good can come.
magis: Christ invites his disciples to follow him and share in his ministry of compassion and healing; the Risen Lord sends them, in his Name, to heal the sick.
The name of Jesus signifies that the very name of God is present in the person of his Son; there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).
The responsibility for the death of Jesus cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today; sinners were the authors of his Passion.
If I have not charity, says the Apostle, I am nothing; charity is superior to all the virtues, the first of the theological virtues.
The signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him; by delivering some from hunger, sickness and death he announced a greater liberation, from sin.
saints: The Friday of Gold, the first Friday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, St Christopher Magallanes, priest, and companions, martyrs of Mexico.

16–22 May: first week of the Season of the Apostles. Mon 17: Mary, Mother of the Church. Thu 20: anniversary of the inauguration of the first Syro-Malabar Bishops' Synod (1993); in the Latin calendar, St Bernardine of Siena. Fri 21: the Friday of Gold; in the Latin calendar, St Christopher Magallanes and companions. Sat 22: in the Latin calendar, St Rita of Cascia. Sun 23: Second Sunday of the Apostles, the feast of the Most Holy Trinity; St Rita, listed for 23 May in the First Set, gives way to the feast (verify locally).
2027-05-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, at the gate of Nain you had compassion on a weeping mother, and at the Beautiful Gate your apostles raised the lame in your holy Name. Pour out on us the Holy Spirit who made them bold and gentle, so that we may look at those who lie at the door and give them what we have: your Name, our hands and our love. Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees; open the eyes of the blind and the hearts of the hard. Make your Church poor in gold and rich in charity, until all the ransomed of the Lord come to Zion with singing, and praise the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

catechism: The apostles share Christ's healing ministry.
kidsaint: St Peter and St John at the Beautiful Gate

Peter and John were two best friends among the apostles. One afternoon, on their way to pray, they met a man who had never been able to walk. He asked for money, but they had none. Peter said, ‘I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you,’ and in the name of Jesus he helped him stand. The man jumped and danced into the Temple, thanking God! That is one reason why this day is often called the Friday of Gold.
2027-05-21.special: The Friday of Gold: first Friday of the Apostles; the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3).
term: The first Friday after Pentecost in the Syriac Churches, recalling the first miracle of the apostles after the coming of the Spirit, the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate. Its name is commonly linked with Peter's words, “I have no silver or gold.” In Malayalam it is known as Swarnavelli.

family.explain: Peter and John were going to pray in the Temple. At the gate sat a man who had never walked; he begged for coins. Peter had no money, but he said, ‘What I have I give you: in the name of Jesus, stand up and walk!’ He took the man's hand, and the man jumped up and went into the Temple praising God. We may not have money to give, but we can always give love, kindness and the name of Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for people who are sick or cannot walk, and for all who care for them.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us give to someone this week that does not cost money?”

illus: In a parish in Thrissur a group of young people noticed that an old man in a wheelchair always sat outside the church during the Qurbana, because there were steps and no one to lift him. One Sunday a college student asked him, ‘Appacha, shall we go in?’ With two friends he carried the chair up the steps. The old man wept through the whole Qurbana. The next month the youth group raised money for a ramp, and the student began to fetch him every Sunday. ‘We had no money at first,’ she said later, ‘but we had arms, and that was enough to begin.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, in your holy Name the lame walk and the dead are raised. Gather us now, poor in gold and rich in your Spirit, and teach us the more excellent way of love. Amen.
share: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees (Isaiah 35:3). Whose weak hands can I strengthen this week?
I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you (Acts 3:6). What do I have that I could give in the name of Jesus?
Love is patient; love is kind (1 Corinthians 13:4). Where am I most impatient or unkind?
When the Lord saw her, he had compassion for her (Luke 7:13). Whom has God placed before my eyes so that I might have compassion?
pm.resp: Lord, in your Name, raise us up.
interc: For the Church, that she may be poor in gold and rich in charity, and give the world the Name of Jesus.
For the disabled, the sick and the elderly, that our parishes may welcome them and help them enter God's house.
For the Jewish people, the descendants of Abraham, that they may receive the blessing promised to all the families of the earth.
For widows and mothers who mourn their children, that the Lord may say to them, Do not weep.
For ourselves, that the Holy Spirit may give us the greatest gift, which is love.
pm.close: Father, in the Name of your Son the apostles raised the lame man at the Beautiful Gate. By the Holy Spirit make us gentle and bold, to give what we have and to love without end. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today our Church keeps the Friday of Gold, the first Friday after Pentecost. It remembers the first miracle the apostles worked after the Holy Spirit came.

Peter and John go to the Temple at three in the afternoon to pray. At the Beautiful Gate a man lame from birth asks them for money. Peter looks at him and says, “Look at us.” Then: “I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you; in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, stand up and walk.” He takes his hand, and the man walks, leaps and praises God.
Isaiah had promised this: “then the lame shall leap like a deer.” The age of the Messiah has come, and the Church continues his work in his Name.

Peter tells the crowd that it was not his power but the God of Abraham who healed the man. He calls them “friends” and says, “I know that you acted in ignorance.” He invites them to repent and receive blessing. The Church blames no people for the Cross; we all need that call to repentance.

Paul tells us the secret behind the miracle: love. Without love, all gifts are nothing. “Love is patient; love is kind… Love never ends.” Peter had no gold, but he had love. And Jesus, at the gate of Nain, had compassion on a widow and gave her son back to her.
So today, do not say, I have nothing to give. You have the name of Jesus, a hand to hold out and a heart to love. That is the gold of the Church. Amen.
kids: Children, Peter and John had no money at all! But they met a man who could not walk, and Peter said, ‘What I have I give you: in the name of Jesus, walk!’ And the man jumped and danced!
You can give something better than money too: a smile, a helping hand, a prayer. That is your gold!

opts.a: At three o'clock, at the Beautiful Gate
intro: Peter and John went up to the Temple at the hour of prayer. At the gate called Beautiful sat a man who had never once walked in. On the Friday of Gold he walks, leaps and praises God inside.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today is the Friday of Gold, when our Church remembers the first miracle of the apostles after Pentecost. Luke begins simply: one day Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, at three o'clock in the afternoon (Acts 3:1). The Holy Spirit had come upon them, yet they kept their hours of prayer.

The Psalm says: evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he will hear my voice (Psalm 55:17). The Spirit does not make prayer unnecessary. He makes it alive. If we want the power of Pentecost, let us also keep a fixed hour of prayer each day.

At the gate called Beautiful sat a man lame from birth. People carried him there every day to beg (Acts 3:2). He lived at the gate of beauty but had never entered. In the old law, those who were lame could not serve at the altar (Leviticus 21:18). He had been left outside all his life. How many people sit at the edges of our parishes: the poor, the disabled, the lonely, those who feel unworthy?

Peter took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. Jumping up, he stood and began to walk, and he entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God (Acts 3:7–8). David once danced before the ark with all his might. This man, who had never walked, now danced into God's house.

That is the gold of the Church: not money, but the name of Jesus that brings people from the gate into the house of God. Let us keep our hour of prayer, notice those who sit at our doors, and bring them in with us to the Holy Qurbana, praising God. Amen.

opts.a: Are you the one who is to come?
intro: Even John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask Jesus: are you the one? Jesus did not scold him. He pointed to what God was doing. Today's Gospel speaks to all who struggle with doubt.

sub: John hears in prison of Jesus' deeds.
He sends two disciples.
How long, O LORD?
points.apply: Bring your honest questions to God in prayer.

points.h: Tell what you have seen and heard
sub: The blind see, the lame walk.
The poor hear good news.
The signs of the Messiah.
points.apply: Write down three things God has done in your life.

points.h: Blessed is anyone who takes no offense
sub: A Messiah different from expectations.
A stone of stumbling.
Love sees in a mirror, dimly, and trusts.
points.apply: When God does not act as you expected, make an act of trust.

concl: Doubt brought to Jesus becomes deeper faith.
His works answer our questions, and love trusts where it cannot yet see.
opts.resolve: This week I will bring my questions to God and remember three things he has done for me.
homily: Dear friends, in today's Gospel even John the Baptist has a question. He is in Herod's prison. He hears of what Jesus is doing, and he sends two of his disciples to ask: are you the one who is to come, or are we to wait for another? (Luke 7:19). The greatest of the prophets wonders.

There is no shame in an honest question brought to God. The Psalms are full of them: how long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Psalm 13:1). God is not offended when we bring our questions to him. He is grieved only when we walk away with them.

Jesus does not argue. He says: go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news brought to them (Luke 7:22). These are the signs Isaiah promised for the anointed one who would bring good news to the oppressed (Isaiah 61:1). The answer to doubt is to look again at what God is doing.

And he adds: blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me (Luke 7:23). John expected a Messiah of fire and judgment. Jesus came with mercy. Isaiah had said that the Lord would become a stone one strikes against. Paul, in today's Epistle, says that now we see in a mirror, dimly, but love bears all things and hopes all things (1 Corinthians 13:7, 12). Love trusts where it cannot yet see.

On this Friday of Gold, when the apostles began to work the same signs in Jesus' name, let us bring our questions to him. Let us write down three things he has done for us. And when he does not act as we expected, let us trust him still, and receive him at the Holy Qurbana. Amen.
